title: What the Bell Calls
subtitle: Wednesday 5 to Friday 14 November 1924: The First Boat, a Town Meeting on Armistice Day, Raising the Bell from the Shelf, and Twenty-Eight Names on Church Point at the Full Moon

setting.name: Carrow Island after the storm, the full moon of November 1924
setting.description: The storm is over. The island is battered, cold, grieving and, for the first time in fifty-three years, told. Orpha Sprague has confessed to the party and given them the 1871 order; she has read the dead their names at her own front door; she has said she will do it again 'before all of them'. The dead still come ashore on every night flood tide and knock at doors with iron, and will until they are laid. The next spring low water is Thursday 13 November at 6:04 p.m., an hour after dark, under a full moon, and the bell will ring then and call one more of the blood unless it is answered. Rule 5 says how to end it: the doors open (done on 29 October, or not), and the bell rung by a hand of the five families' blood once for each of the dead, as each name is spoken aloud before the people of the island. Three things stand in the way. The island has to agree to stand on the Point and hear its grandfathers named for what they did, and some of it will not. The bell is still in the drowned church's tower on the Shelf, under four feet of water at a spring low and eight at an ordinary one, and must be raised or reached. And the names must all be there, every one, twenty-eight of them, and the party may not yet know that they have only twenty-seven.
setting.atmosphere: After the storm, the clearest weather of the year: hard blue sky, a north wind with ice in it, the bay sparkling and the mainland hills white with the first snow. Wreckage on every beach, smashed traps, a schooner on her side below the Head, the Store's salt fish spread on the wharf to dry. The island quiet, working, and watching itself. The nights are bright with the moon growing toward full, and on every flood tide the dead walk up out of the silver water and stand in the lanes, and the Harbor no longer hides behind its shutters to watch them but stands in its doorways, in its coats, and looks at them, and some people have begun to call them by name. The ending should feel like a funeral that has been waited for for fifty-three years: solemn, frightening, cold, and, at the very end, a relief so large that grown men weep.

keyLocations.name: The Grange hall: the special town meeting
keyLocations.description: Called by the First Selectman at Orpha Sprague's request for Tuesday 11 November at two in the afternoon, Armistice Day, by notice nailed on the Store porch: 'To see if the town will hear Mrs. Orpha Sprague on the matter of the Point, and act thereon.' Every grown person on the island comes. The hall's stove is roaring, the benches are full, the windows are steamed, and the wreck's French sailors stand at the back, not understanding a word and understanding everything.
features: The stage and Ellery Wyman's table, with the town's warrant book and the 1871 order laid on it
The benches: the five families' descendants on one side by long habit, the Point families' few on the other, the incomers and the married-in in between
The honor roll of the island's war dead on the wall, with a wreath on it for Armistice Day
encounters: Marcellus Tibbetts and the families who do not want the names said
Mattie Grindle, who has waited her whole life for this and does not know what to do now it has come
secrets: What Orpha says (the GM can read the controlFile's theTruth aloud in her voice): the fever, the order, the spikes, the Bar, her father's no, the four hours, the bell, the probate, the iron over the doors, Zeb Lunt, 'and I held the lantern, and I have said nothing for fifty-three years, and every one of you who has lost someone to the sea since August has lost them to my silence as much as to anything'. Then she lays the order on the table and says she will stand on the Point on Thursday at the bottom of the tide and ring for every one of them with her own hand, and she asks the island to come and hear.

Orpha's restitution: she signs, at the table, before the meeting, a deed giving the Sprague share of the old Point fishing privilege back to the heirs of Thomas Grindle, which is Mattie, and asks the other four families to do the same. This is the hardest moment of the meeting, and it is not part of the rite; the bell does not care about property. The island does.

Marcellus Tibbetts's objection, and the reasons under it: he owns the weirs on the old Point privilege, which feed his family; his grandfather Eliphalet's name is on the order; and he believes, honestly, that the answering ringing works and can go on forever, so why shame the dead for nothing? 'We'll ring every big tide till the end of the world, and keep our grandfathers decent in their graves.' He is not wrong that it would work. He is wrong about what it would cost: one person of the blood every time a ringer is ill, or late, or tired, or dead, for as long as there is a Carrow.

keyLocations.name: The Church Shelf and the derrick lighter Hercules
keyLocations.description: The Carrow Granite Company's old derrick lighter, the Hercules, a seventy-foot flat-bottomed sloop with a wooden derrick and a steam hoisting engine, has lain at the Wyman wharf since the quarry closed in 1909, used once a year to set mooring stones. Ellery Wyman owns her. She can lift eight tons. Over the Shelf at the bottom of a spring tide, with a diver to put a sling on it, she can lift a nine-hundred-pound bell out of a rotten tower and set it on the Point. The Bonne Chance's crew, idle until a steamer can tow their schooner off, will crew her for nothing.
features: The Hercules's steam engine, which has not been fired since 1923 and needs a mechanic and a day
Galen Coombs's deep-sea dress, air pump and hose, and Arno Farr, who will not go down again
The drowned church's tower: open at the top, the bell hanging tilted in its rotten frame, four feet under at the spring low on 12 November
If Galen's charge brought the tower down on 29 October: the bell lies on the Shelf among the wreckage of the tower, mouth up, and is easier to sling
encounters: The dive: whoever goes down in the dress, in the green dark, among weed and timber, with the dead in the pews below and Ardelia Vining in the vestibule
The lift: steam, chain, a rotten frame, a nine-hundred-pound bell and a swell
secrets: If the doors were buried by Galen's charge on 29 October, the diver must first clear them (two hours' work with a pry bar and a line to the Hercules's winch to drag timber away, over two low waters) and draw the spikes under water (Athletics DC 16 per two, in the dress). It is the hardest thing in the campaign and the GM should let it take everything the party have.

The bell in the tower rings, faintly, under the diver's hands, whenever it is touched; anyone in the dress hears it through the helmet as a voice saying their family name, and if they are of the blood, they must make a Charisma save DC 13 or begin walking, very slowly, along the Shelf toward the church doors; the tender on the hose line must haul them up.
Ardelia Vining (Bound Spirit statistics) watches the dive from the vestibule and does not interfere. If the diver speaks to her by name, she points up at the tower.

keyLocations.name: Church Point at the full moon
keyLocations.description: The Point on Thursday 13 November: the grass white with frost, the cellar holes of the old settlement black, the Bar dry, the moon rising over Carrow Head, and at the end of the Point, where the land slopes down to the sea, the bell, if it has been raised, hung in a frame of spars lashed together by Peleg and the Bonne Chance's crew, with a rope. Around it the whole island, a hundred and forty people with lanterns, and beyond it, the Shelf, under silver water, and the drowned church's tower just showing.
features: The bell in its frame of spars, and its rope
A table carried down from the Grange hall, with the order, Zeb's ringing book and a lantern on it
The line of lanterns along the Bar, and five more that nobody is holding
encounters: The dead, coming up out of the sea at the bottom of the tide to stand on the slope below the Point and listen
The call: whoever rings, of the blood, will feel it
secrets: THE TWENTY-EIGHTH NAME. The order in the Sprague Bible has twenty-three names, the twenty-three of 1871. The 1924 three are on Spruce Hill. Philena Farr is on her stone. But the bell took one more: Asahel Wyman, Seth Wyman's brother, in November 1871, before Joel Vining learned to answer it. He is named in Vining's letter ('it took Asahel Wyman in November') and on the flyleaf of Zeb Lunt's ringing book, and nowhere else. A party that rings twenty-seven will find, at the last stroke, that the bell does not stop: it swings on by itself, slowly, and Ardelia Vining, at the water's edge, says: 'One more. You have left one of us out. He was theirs, and he was ours.' The party have as long as the tide is low, about twenty minutes, to find the name. (Zeb's book, if they have it, on the table; Ellery Wyman, who knows his own family's stones, if asked: 'There's a stone in our plot to an Asahel. No dates. I never knew who he was.')

THE RINGER IS CALLED. When the bell begins to sway by itself at 6:04 p.m., the one of the blood nearest it is called, and that is whoever has taken the rope. They feel their family name in the bell and the pull of the sea, and must make a Charisma save DC 15 at each name or let go and walk toward the water; friends holding them, a Chaplain's Steady Now, a Faithful origin's advantage and a Sensitive's Quiet Mind all help, and the island can hold them. The rope must be rung by a hand of the blood: if Orpha cannot finish, Peleg can, or Ellery, or Dr. Thurlow, or Galen, or Clyde, and the names go on from where they stopped.

What happens at the end (if every name is spoken and rung for, before the island): the last stroke of the raised bell is answered, from under the sea, by a single stroke of no bell at all, enormous and soft, and then silence. The dead on the slope are seen, by those who look, walking up the Bar in the moonlight among the lanterns, past the five lights, which go out, and then they are not there. Everyone present drops to 0 Dread. The bell never rings again under the sea, and nobody of the blood is ever called again. Mattie Grindle sits down on the frost and laughs until she cries.

keyLocations.name: The wharf and the first boat
keyLocations.description: Wednesday 5 November, the Viola R. back on her run, deep-laden with mail, coal, kerosene, the island's orders and whoever is coming back. Behind her, on Thursday 6 November, the Coast Guard cutter from Rockland with a grapnel to find the parted telephone cable, a lieutenant with questions about the Bonne Chance and her cargo, and a Portland Press reporter who has heard that ghosts walk on Carrow.
features: Whatever a returning character arranged in db-scenario-003: a Rockland diver and his dress, Miss Prudence Vining with her uncle's letters, the Mariner's files
The Coast Guard's 125-foot cutter, too big for the harbor, lying off with a launch
encounters: Lieutenant (j.g.) Harold Scamman, U.S. Coast Guard, polite, efficient and not a fool, looking for a Saint-Pierre schooner's cargo and a woman named Tolman
Myrtle Haskins of the Portland paper, young, sharp, kind, and a danger to everything the island is trying to do
secrets: Scamman knows the Bonne Chance's cargo is in the island's cellars and does not much care: he wants the schooner's master for the record and Peg Tolman for a warrant from Boothbay. The island protects whoever it has decided is its own (Standing +2 or better: nobody has ever heard of a Peg Tolman; Standing 0 or less: she is pointed out).

The reporter, if she gets her story, prints CARROW'S DROWNED WALK by Saturday, and the island will be full of Boston tourists by spring. Imogen Lisle, Len Garrity or Pearl Haverty, each of whom knows how a story is told, can talk her into a different one: about the bell, a ballad, a storm and an old woman who told the truth, which is also true, and which she prints, and which the island can live with.

synopsis: The first boat after the storm brings back anyone who went ashore, the Coast Guard comes for the cable and the rum schooner's cargo, and a Portland reporter comes for the ghosts. The dead still walk the lanes on every night flood, and the island stands in its doorways now and calls some of them by name. Orpha Sprague asks for a special town meeting, and on Armistice Day, Tuesday 11 November, in the Grange hall, she tells the island what the five Proprietor families did in 1871, lays the order with their five signatures on the table, gives the Sprague share of the old Point fishing privilege back to Mattie Grindle, and asks the island to come to the Point on Thursday at the bottom of the tide and hear her ring for every one of the dead. Marcellus Tibbetts, whose living depends on the Point weirs and whose grandfather signed the order, argues that the answering ringing can go on forever and keep their grandfathers decent; the party must help the island decide. Meanwhile the bell must be raised: Ellery Wyman's old granite derrick lighter, the Hercules, fired up and crewed by the wrecked French sailors, Galen Coombs's deep-sea dress and a diver brave enough to go down into the drowned church's tower at the spring low on Wednesday 12 November, with the dead in the pews below and the bell saying the diver's family name. On Thursday 13 November, at 6:04 p.m. under a full moon, the whole island stands on Church Point with lanterns around the raised bell in a frame of spars, the dead come up out of the sea to stand on the slope below and listen, and Orpha Sprague, held up by her neighbors against the bell's call, reads the names and rings once for each. If every one is there, twenty-eight of them, including Asahel Wyman, whom the bell took in November 1871 and whose name is only in Joel Vining's letter and Zeb Lunt's book, the last stroke is answered once from under the sea, the dead walk up the Bar in the moonlight and are gone, and the bell never calls anyone again.
hook: Wednesday 5 November, the Store porch, noon. A notice in Ellery Wyman's hand is nailed beside the tide table: SPECIAL TOWN MEETING. The inhabitants of Carrow are warned to meet at the Grange Hall on Tuesday the 11th inst. at 2 o'clock P.M., to see if the town will hear Mrs. Orpha Sprague on the matter of the Point, and act thereon. Under it someone has written in pencil: AND RING. Under that, in another hand: NO. And under that, in a third hand, small and neat, the names of twenty-three people who died in 1871, which someone has copied from somewhere, and which no one has dared to rub out.

conclusions.conclusion: F. The bell is laid by the doors opened, and every one of the dead named and rung for by the five families' blood, before the island (Rule 5)
clues: F1: the ballad's last verse in Zeb Lunt's book (db-scenario-001 or 002)
F3: Ardelia Vining: 'Say who we were. Say it where they can hear' (db-scenario-002 and 003)
Orpha's reading at her door on 3 November sent the dead back to the sea for a night but did not lay them: not rung, not before the island (db-scenario-003)
F5: the doors opened on 29 October ended the call but the bell still rings at every spring low (db-scenario-002 and this scenario)

conclusions.conclusion: The twenty-eighth name: Asahel Wyman, whom the bell took in November 1871
clues: Joel Vining's letter: 'it took Asahel Wyman in November' (db-scenario-002)
Zeb Lunt's ringing book flyleaf: twenty-five names, the order's twenty-three, Asahel Wyman and Philena Farr (db-scenario-001)
A stone in the Wyman plot on Spruce Hill to 'Asahel', with no dates, which Ellery never understood (Spruce Hill)
Ardelia Vining at the water's edge: 'One more. He was theirs, and he was ours' (the Point, if the party miss it)

conclusions.conclusion: D. The island hears what the five families did, from one of their own, before all its people
clues: D5: Orpha Sprague's confession (db-scenario-003, and again at the town meeting)
D6: the 1871 order with the five signatures (the Sprague Bible, the meeting's table)
D1: Nehemiah Pinkham's log, which Oren reads aloud at the meeting if Orpha falters (the Light)
Joel Vining's letter, which Miss Prudence Vining reads aloud at the meeting if she has come out on the boat (Rockland)

acts.title: After the Storm
acts.description: Wednesday 5 to Monday 10 November. The island cleans up and the mainland arrives: the first boat, the Coast Guard, the reporter. Characters who went ashore come back with what they arranged. The dead walk on every night flood (about 12:40 a.m. on the 5th, an hour later each night), and the island now watches them from its doorways and, increasingly, calls them by name; the party should see that the names work, and that they only work for a night. Clyde Tibbetts's fate is decided. Peg Tolman's warrant comes looking for her. Orpha Sprague asks Ellery for the special town meeting. And the party, with Peleg, Galen and Ellery, must plan how to get the bell out of the sea by Thursday.
objectives: Deal with the Coast Guard lieutenant and the Portland reporter so that the island can do what it has to do in peace
Decide what happens to Clyde Tibbetts
Make sure every one of the twenty-eight names is known and written down
Get the Hercules's engine running and the deep-sea dress ready, and choose a diver

scenes.name: The Lieutenant and the Reporter
scenes.description: Thursday 6 November. The cutter lies off; her launch comes in to the wharf with Lieutenant Scamman and two seamen, and with them, having talked her way aboard in Rockland, Myrtle Haskins of the Portland paper. Scamman wants the Bonne Chance's master, the cargo if he can find it without trouble, the cable mended, and, from a Boothbay warrant, a woman named Margaret Tolman. Myrtle wants the drowned walking. Let the party and the island handle them: the island closes ranks for its own (Standing decides who that is); Scamman is decent and can be reasoned with; Myrtle is young, kind and ambitious and will print something. What she prints is the party's to shape.
scenes.readAloud: The Coast Guard launch comes in to the wharf in a smother of spray, with a white ensign snapping at her stern and a lieutenant standing in her bow in a bridge coat with his gloves in his hand, looking at the island the way a man looks at a house he has been told is full of smugglers and suspects is full of grandmothers. Beside him, holding her hat on with one hand and a notebook in the other, is a young woman in a camel coat who is already writing. 'Lieutenant Scamman, Coast Guard,' he says, stepping up onto the wharf. 'I'm here about a cable, a schooner and a lady. This is Miss Haskins of the Portland paper. I'm afraid she's here about ghosts.'

skillChecks.success: Scamman takes the Bonne Chance's master's statement, mends the cable, inventories a cargo that has somehow become forty cases of salt herring, and says, looking at the sky, that he has no description of any Margaret Tolman that would fit anybody he can see. He leaves on Saturday. (Advantage if the party saved the schooner's crew; automatic at Standing +3.)
skillChecks.failure: Scamman is polite and thorough. He finds twenty cases, which the island did not hide well enough, and asks Peg Tolman, by name, to come to Rockland with him on Saturday to answer a warrant. She can go, run, or be hidden by the island.

skillChecks.success: Myrtle Haskins gets a story about a church bell, a ballad, a storm, a rescue at the Light and an old woman who told the truth about her family, and prints it, and it is beautiful, and nobody comes to Carrow to look for ghosts. (Imogen Lisle, Len Garrity, or Pearl Haverty's Séance Trade give advantage; telling her the plain truth and asking her to leave out the dead also works, with Persuasion DC 12, because she is kind.)
skillChecks.failure: Myrtle Haskins sees the dead in the lane on Thursday night from the Store's porch, and her paper prints CARROW'S DROWNED WALK on Saturday. The island's Standing for the party drops 1 if they brought her, and there will be visitors in the spring.

skillChecks.success: Scamman has been on the rum patrol two years and lost two men off Boothbay in a fog. He does not want to arrest anybody on this island. He wants to go home with something to write down.
skillChecks.failure: A Coast Guard officer with a warrant. Treat him as one.

scenes.name: What to Do About Clyde
scenes.description: Clyde Tibbetts, ashore from the wreck, has been hiding in Verna's attic with a cracked rib. Galen Coombs wants $1,400 or Clyde's hide; Merrymeeting Life wants him prosecuted for fraud, which Len Garrity can arrange with one letter; Verna wants him back and both of them off the island; and Clyde, who is of the blood, will be called on Thursday if he is nearest the Point, and is terrified. Let the party choose. A good ending: Clyde stands on the Point on Thursday with the island, holds the rope for the Tibbetts names if Orpha falters, works off his debt to Galen raising the bell, and Len writes a report that saves Merrymeeting $2,000 and leaves out the warrant. A hard ending: he goes to Rockland in irons on Scamman's launch. Either is fair.
scenes.readAloud: Clyde Tibbetts is sitting on the edge of a bed in Verna's attic with his ribs strapped and a blanket round his shoulders, a thin sandy man with a weak chin and frightened eyes, and Verna stands between him and the door with her arms folded as if she has decided she is going to hold him on the shore again, for as long as it takes. 'I know what I done,' he says, before anyone speaks. 'I know. I heard my name in it, on the thirty-first, and Verna held me, and I come back, and I thought, next time she won't be able to. And I owed Galen. So I run.' He looks at the floor. 'And then the sea put me back. Right under the light. Right in front of them. You know what they looked like, standing in the surf, waiting? Like they was glad to see me.'

skillChecks.success: Clyde is a coward and knows it, and is more ashamed of it now than of the fraud. He would do anything to be allowed to be brave once.
skillChecks.failure: A frightened little cheat. Whatever happens to him, he earned.

skillChecks.success: Galen Coombs agrees to take Clyde's debt out in work on the Hercules, and Clyde agrees to stand on the Point on Thursday, and Verna agrees to let him. Len Garrity, if he is the one who decides, writes the report as he chooses.
skillChecks.failure: Galen will not be moved: $1,400 or Clyde leaves the island. It can still be settled with money ($1,400 is about what Peg Tolman made on the whisky).

skillChecks.success: 'Like they was glad to see me.' You have seen them too. You can bear it.
skillChecks.failure: You remember the faces in the surf below the Head, and you understand that they were glad. Gain 1 Dread.

scenes.name: Every One of Them
scenes.description: Any day this week, at the Store's back-room table or the Light's kitchen: the party lay out every source for the names and make the list. The order: twenty-three. The vestibule plaster: seventeen of them. Lois Grindle's list in Mattie's hymnbook: twenty-two, missing one Gloucester man (Elias Dunbar). The Mariner's crew list: the six Gloucester men. The cenotaphs on Spruce Hill: nine. The stones on Spruce Hill: Philena Farr, Enoch Farr, Esther Thurlow, Jotham Wyman. Zeb Lunt's flyleaf: twenty-five: the twenty-three, Philena Farr, and Asahel Wyman. Joel Vining's letter: Asahel Wyman, 'in November'. The reward for doing this carefully is the twenty-eighth name; the party who do it carelessly will find it on the Point at the worst moment. Ellery Wyman, asked about Asahel, says there is a stone in the Wyman plot to an 'Asahel' with no dates, and goes very quiet.
scenes.readAloud: The Store's back room is cold and smells of old paper and lamp oil, and the long table is covered: the order in Seth Wyman's hand, with its five signatures; Zeb Lunt's ringing book open at the flyleaf; a rubbing of the vestibule plaster on butcher paper; Lois Grindle's hymnbook with its pencilled list; Miss Vining's letter; the Mariner's crew list copied out in Willard Hosmer's hand; a sheet of names from the stones on Spruce Hill. Mattie Grindle sits at one end with her arms folded and says nothing. Ellery Wyman sits at the other with his reading glasses on and his finger moving down the order, name by name, and his lips moving. When he gets to the bottom he starts again at the top.

skillChecks.success: You check every source against every other and find that the order has twenty-three, the stones add four, and Zeb's flyleaf and Vining's letter have one more that is nowhere else: Asahel Wyman. Twenty-eight. (Seen It in a Book or Folklorist's interview with Thankful Lunt gives this without a roll: 'Zeb always said there was one before the ringing started.')
skillChecks.failure: You make a careful list from the order and the stones: twenty-seven names. It looks complete. It is not.

skillChecks.success: Ellery Wyman, reading the order over and over, is not checking it. He is reading his great-grandfather's handwriting. When you ask, he says, 'Seth Wyman wrote this. In his own hand. And he wrote the Record of the Gale, that says they sheltered. He wrote both.'
skillChecks.failure: The First Selectman is checking the list.

skillChecks.success: Mattie Grindle reads you her great-grandparents' names off Lois's list, and their ages, and what Lois said about each of them: Thomas could whistle like a thrush, Rhoda kept bees. Do this for each name you can and the island, on Thursday, hears not a list but people. (Not needed for the rite; it is for the island.)
skillChecks.failure: Mattie does not want to talk today. She leaves the hymnbook on the table.

encounters: Lieutenant Scamman and two Coast Guard seamen (Deputy Sheriff statistics if it comes to that, which it should not)
The Drowned in the lanes on the night floods: no longer frightening the island into its houses, and still dangerous to anyone who stands in a doorway against them

acts.title: Armistice Day
acts.description: Tuesday 11 November and Wednesday 12 November. The town meeting, and the raising of the bell. On Tuesday afternoon, while the island is in the Grange hall, the Hercules is getting up steam at the Wyman wharf under Peg Tolman or Peleg Sprague, with the French sailors at her lines. On Wednesday, at the dawn spring low water (5:21 a.m., a moon still high in the west), she goes round to the Shelf with the deep-sea dress aboard, and someone goes down into the drowned church's tower to put a sling on the bell.
objectives: Help the town meeting decide to stand on the Point and hear the names
Fire up the Hercules and get her to the Shelf
Dive to the tower, sling the bell and bring it up
Set the bell in a frame on Church Point

scenes.name: Mrs. Orpha Sprague on the Matter of the Point
scenes.description: The Grange hall, two in the afternoon. Ellery Wyman reads the warrant and calls Orpha, who is carried up the steps in a chair by Peleg and Galen and stands at the table on her cane, and speaks for twenty minutes without notes. Then she lays the order on the table, signs the deed returning the Sprague share of the Point privilege to Mattie Grindle, and sits. The room is silent. Then Marcellus Tibbetts stands and says, with real pain, why he will not have his grandfather's name shouted on the Point for nothing, when the ringing works and can go on forever. Others agree. Let the party and their friends answer: Kingsley Trask on what the ringing costs (one of the blood every time a ringer fails, forever); Oren Pinkham reading his father's page; Dr. Thurlow on Esther; Mattie Grindle, who stands up and says only, 'I don't want your weirs, Marcellus. I want my great-grandmother's name said out loud on the Point by a Sprague. That's all'; Ellery Wyman, who in the end stands and says that his great-grandfather wrote both the order and the lie, in the same hand, and that he will stand on the Point. The vote is by standing: the GM decides from what is said, but a party with Standing +1 or more who speak honestly should carry it.
scenes.readAloud: She stands at the table on the stage with both hands on her cane, ninety pounds of black silk and white hair, and the Grange hall, a hundred and forty people packed shoulder to shoulder with their breath steaming, is so quiet you can hear the stove tick. On the wall behind her is the island's honor roll from the war, with a wreath of spruce on it for Armistice Day. She does not look at any paper. 'My father was Captain Hezekiah Sprague,' she says, 'and on the ninth of October 1871 he signed an order, and on the eighteenth I held his lantern on the Bar while he did a wicked thing, and I have been silent about it for fifty-three years. I am going to tell you what it was. Then I am going to ask you to do something, and you may say no.'

skillChecks.success: You answer Marcellus Tibbetts without contempt: that the ringing works, and that it has already failed once in 1898 and five times this year, and will fail again; that nobody is asking him to give up his weirs, only to stand on the Point and hear his grandfather's name; that the dead are not asking for anyone's blood, only to be named. The island stands. Marcellus stands last, and slowly. (Advantage for each companion who spoke; advantage if Standing is +2 or more.)
skillChecks.failure: The island is divided, and the vote is close, and it carries by four. Marcellus Tibbetts and a dozen others do not come to the Point; the rite does not need them, but Marcellus is of the blood, and on Thursday, at the bell, he is called, walking down the shore road from his house in his slippers, and someone must go and hold him.

skillChecks.success: The truth, told plainly, in a warm room full of people, by an old woman. You have heard it before. You hear it now as the island hears it, and you keep your seat.
skillChecks.failure: The truth of it, again, in a room full of the grandchildren and great-grandchildren of the people who did it and the people it was done to, sitting on the same benches. Gain 1 Dread. (A character who has already paid for the truth of the bell this scenario does not pay twice.)

skillChecks.success: Halfway through Orpha's speech Hosea Farr gets up from the five families' side of the hall, walks across, and sits down on the Point side next to Mattie Grindle, without a word. Two others follow him. Nobody comments.
skillChecks.failure: A frozen room. You cannot tell what they are thinking.

scenes.name: Steam on the Hercules
scenes.description: Tuesday into Wednesday. The Hercules's boiler has not been fired for a year and her derrick's falls are rotten. Peg Tolman or Peleg Sprague, with the French sailors, Galen's crew and anyone else, get her going: scale the boiler, re-reeve the falls with new manila from the Store, test the hoist on a mooring stone. Then, at four in the morning on Wednesday, she goes round from the Harbor to the Shelf under steam and her own sail, in the moonlight, with the dress and pump on deck, and anchors fore and aft over the drowned church with her derrick swung out over the tower. A good, practical, warm scene: everyone on the island who can work, working, for once, on the same thing.
scenes.readAloud: By midnight the Hercules is alive: steam hissing from her donkey boiler, the derrick's mast creaking, a lantern at every corner, the French sailors singing something in the dark as they haul on the new falls, Galen Coombs's young men coiling hose, and Peg Tolman with her head in the engine and grease to her elbows swearing in two languages. Peleg is up the derrick mast with a marlinspike. Mattie Grindle is splicing an eye in a sling with hands that do not hesitate. Ellery Wyman, who owns the old lighter and has not set foot on her in ten years, is standing on her deck in his best coat, watching, and every few minutes he takes the coat off, and then puts it on again.

skillChecks.success: The boiler holds pressure, the hoisting engine turns over, the derrick lifts a two-ton mooring stone clear of the wharf and sets it down again. She will do. (Teamster or Grease Under the Nails gives advantage.)
skillChecks.failure: A tube in the boiler gives way at midnight with a scream of steam; nobody is hurt, it takes until three to plug it, and she will lift, but slowly: the bell will take two hours to come up instead of one.

skillChecks.success: You re-reeve the falls by lantern light, forty feet up a creaking derrick in a cold wind, and they run true.
skillChecks.failure: A block jams and someone must go up and clear it, and slips, and is caught by the safety line, and hangs there swearing for a minute before they are hauled in. (1d6 bludgeoning and a story for the Store stove.)

skillChecks.success: You con the Hercules round the island in the moonlight and anchor her over the tower without touching the Shelf. (Oren Pinkham or Mattie Grindle do this without a roll.)
skillChecks.failure: She touches on the edge of the Shelf and swings; it takes half an hour to get her anchored square, and the low water will not wait.

scenes.name: Down into the Tower
scenes.description: Wednesday 12 November, about 5:00 to 5:45 a.m., the spring low water at 5:21, under a setting moon. The diver goes down in Galen's dress: copper helmet, canvas suit, lead boots, a hose to the hand pump on deck where two people pump and a tender holds the line. Arno Farr will not go. Peleg will, or any of the party, or Galen himself. It is four feet down to the top of the tower and twelve to the bell's crown inside it: green dark, the lantern on the helmet a blur, weed waving, the rotten timbers of the belfry, and the bell hanging tilted in its frame. Get the sling round its crown and the hook in, signal, and the derrick takes the weight; the frame gives way and the bell swings free and up. While the diver works the bell hums under their hands, and through the helmet they hear their family name; if of the blood, Charisma save DC 13 each minute or begin walking along the top of the tower toward the drop into the nave, and the tender must haul. Looking down through the belfry floor into the nave, the diver sees the dead in their pews, all looking up. Ardelia Vining is in the vestibule, and if spoken to, points up. When the bell breaks the surface, streaming, green, in the first grey of dawn, everyone on the Hercules cheers, and on the Point, where half the island has come to watch, they cheer too, and then are silent.
scenes.readAloud: The water closes over the helmet's window and the world goes green and then black. There is the hiss of air in the helmet, the thud of your own heart, the far creak of the pump on deck, and your breath fogging the glass. The lantern makes a small brown room in the water. You go down the rope hand over hand, weed brushing the window like hair, and your lead boots touch something soft and give: the top of the tower, timbers furred with mussel and weed. You climb in over the rotten rail. And there in front of you, in the brown light, tilted in its broken frame, enormous, green and black, is the bell. You put out your glove to it. It hums. You feel it through the glove and the suit and your bones, a long low note, and inside the helmet, quite clearly, in a voice like your own mother's, someone is saying your name.

skillChecks.success: You get the sling round the bell's crown, under the canons, and the hook through both eyes, and give the line four pulls. Above you the derrick takes the strain, the frame groans and splits, and the bell swings free past you in a cloud of silt and goes up into the green, and you go up after it. (Two failures in a row and the tender should haul the diver up for air and someone else must go.)
skillChecks.failure: The sling slips off the crown. Your hands are cold through the gloves and the silt is everywhere. Try again.

skillChecks.success: Your family name, in your mother's voice, from the bell. You hold on to the frame and say your own first name back, aloud, inside the helmet, until it stops.
skillChecks.failure: You let go of the frame and step toward the edge of the belfry floor and the long drop into the dark nave where the dead are looking up, and above you on deck the tender feels the line go slack and hauls with everything he has. (Only for divers of the blood. The tender's Athletics DC 12 brings you up before you step off.)

skillChecks.success: Through the broken belfry floor you see the nave below, and the pews, and the faces, all turned up toward you, and you finish your work.
skillChecks.failure: The faces in the pews, turned up toward you. Gain 1 Dread. Signal to come up, or stay and finish; your choice.

encounters: The town meeting: no combat; a debate, with the vote decided by what the party and their friends say

The dive: the bell's call through the helmet (Charisma save), the cold, the dark, the dead in the pews below; Ardelia Vining in the vestibule (Bound Spirit statistics; she does not interfere and may help)
If the doors were buried on 29 October: two extra low waters of underwater work on the doors (see keyLocations), with the Drowned in the nave behind them pressing at the cracks as the spikes come out

acts.title: Before All the Island
acts.description: Thursday 13 November, dusk to the turn of the tide. The bell is on the Point, hung in a frame of spars at the top of the slope above the Shelf, with a rope. A table from the Grange hall beside it with the order, the list of twenty-eight, Zeb's ringing book and a lantern. The island comes down the shore road and out along the Bar at dusk with lanterns, all of them, a hundred and forty, the five families and the Point families and the incomers and the French sailors, and stands in a great half circle on the frosty grass. The full moon rises over the Head. At 5:40 the dead come up out of the sea onto the slope below the Point, all of them, and stand in the moonlight, waiting. At 6:04, the low water, the bell begins to sway by itself. Orpha Sprague takes the rope. Run it name by name.
objectives: Get the whole island to the Point, and keep those of the blood who are not ringing held
Hold the ringer against the call while every name is spoken and rung
Speak and ring every one of the twenty-eight, including Asahel Wyman

scenes.name: The Island Comes to the Point
scenes.description: Dusk. The procession down the shore road, past the Tibbetts house and Peleg's boat shed, out along the Bar, onto the Point among the cellar holes. Let the party see who has come: Ellery Wyman in his best coat; Hosea Farr carrying his father; Sophronia Coombs; Verna and Clyde, holding hands; Galen and his crew, sober; Thankful Lunt in a wheelbarrow pushed by her grandson-in-law, insisting; Mattie Grindle; Kingsley Trask in his surplice; Oren Pinkham, who has left Jonas on the light, or Jonas, who has left Oren; the French sailors with their caps off; Marcellus Tibbetts, last, alone, if the meeting went well. Miss Prudence Vining, if she came out on the boat, on Kingsley's arm. The five lights at the head of the Bar, which everyone can see tonight. And then, at 5:40, the dead, coming up out of the silver water below the Point, and standing on the slope in the moonlight, all of them, and the island, which has been afraid of them for two weeks, standing above them on the grass, and nobody running.
scenes.readAloud: They come out along the Bar in the dusk with lanterns, the whole island, a long swinging line of lights on the gravel with the sea quiet on both sides and the moon coming up enormous and orange over Carrow Head. Nobody talks. On the Point they spread out across the frosty grass among the old cellar holes in a great half circle around the bell, which hangs in its frame of lashed spars at the top of the slope, green and black and streaming still, with its rope hanging down. At the head of the Bar, behind them all, five small lights stand in a row that nobody is holding. And at twenty minutes to six, down the slope below the Point, where the sea is drawing back off the weed, the dead come up out of the water: one, and three, and ten, and all of them, men in smocks and oilskins and women in long wet dresses, barefoot, streaming silver in the moonlight, and stand on the slope in a crowd, below the island, looking up at it. And the island, standing on the grass with its lanterns, looks back.

skillChecks.success: The dead, all of them, at once, in the moonlight. You know every rule they keep. You stand with the island.
skillChecks.failure: So many. Gain 1 Dread. Somebody beside you takes your hand, and you let them.

skillChecks.success: Along the line, people are starting to step back from the edge of the slope, and someone at the back asks, too loudly, what happens now, and is hushed. You go along the line saying, quietly, that the dead are not here for anyone, that they have come to listen, that nobody needs to move; and the line holds. (Kingsley Trask's Steady Now on anyone who is wavering; Pearl Haverty's Read the Room tells you who.)
skillChecks.failure: Three or four people break and run back along the Bar. Nobody stops them. The rite does not need them, but the island will remember who ran.

skillChecks.success: The dead are looking at faces. Each one of them is looking for someone in the crowd, and some of them find who they were looking for: a Grindle, a Lunt, a Kenniston descendant. Mattie Grindle stands very straight, looking down at a man in a smock and a woman with her hair under a cap.
skillChecks.failure: A crowd of the dead in the moonlight. You cannot read them.

scenes.name: Twenty-Eight
scenes.description: 6:04 p.m. The bell begins to sway by itself in its frame, with no hand on it, and gives a single soft note, and the call comes: Orpha Sprague, at the rope, of the blood, feels it. She reads the first name from the list in a thin, clear voice, 'Ardelia Vining', and pulls, and the bell rings, enormous in the frosty air, and at the bottom of the slope a slight woman in grey looks up. Name by name. Each name, the bell; each name, one of the dead turns its face up to the island. Orpha must make a Charisma save DC 15 at every name or let go and walk toward the slope; she has advantage while two people hold her and the Faithful advantage does not apply (she is Old Family), but a Chaplain's Steady Now, a Sensitive's Quiet Mind or a friend's voice saying her name gives a fresh save. If she fails, the people holding her must win a contested Athletics check against the call (+4) or she slips them; if she cannot go on, someone of the blood takes the rope and goes on from the next name: Peleg, Ellery, Dr. Thurlow, Galen, Clyde, Hosea. Others of the blood in the crowd feel the call too, faintly, and the island holds them. After each name, if the party gave Mattie's stories to the reader, she says one thing about each: 'Thomas Grindle, who could whistle like a thrush.' Twenty-three, then Asahel Wyman, then Philena Farr, then Enoch Farr, Esther Thurlow and Jotham Wyman. If the twenty-eighth is missing, the bell swings on by itself after the twenty-seventh, and Ardelia, at the water's edge, says 'One more'; the party have until the tide turns, about 6:30, to find Asahel.
scenes.readAloud: At four minutes past six, in the moonlight, in a silence so complete that you can hear the frost creaking in the grass, the bell begins to move. Nobody is touching it. It swings, slowly, in its frame of spars, once, and gives a low soft note that you feel in the ground, and below the Point every one of the dead lifts its head. Orpha Sprague, in her black silk and her shawl, with Peleg holding one arm and Mattie Grindle the other, takes the rope in both her small hands. Her face changes: she has heard her name in it. Then she looks down at the paper Ellery Wyman is holding up to the lantern for her, and in a thin clear voice that carries over the whole Point, she reads: 'Ardelia Vining.' And pulls. And the bell rings out over the island and the sea, enormous, and at the edge of the water, at the bottom of the slope, a slight woman in grey with her hair down looks up at the old woman on the rope, and the two of them look at each other for a long moment across fifty-three years.

skillChecks.success: The ringer holds: the name, the stroke, the next name. (Roll for each name, or in groups of five to keep the scene moving; the GM should let the names themselves be read aloud at the table, one by one, all twenty-eight.)
skillChecks.failure: The ringer lets go of the rope and takes a step toward the slope, smiling. The holders must hold (contested Athletics, the call at +4), or the next of the blood must take the rope, and the next name must be read.

skillChecks.success: You hold her. She is ninety pounds and as strong as the sea and she leans toward the water with her eyes on the dead and you hold her with your heels in the frozen grass, and someone says her name, Orpha, Orpha, and she comes back, and reads the next.
skillChecks.failure: She slips out of your arms and takes three steps down the slope before Peleg catches her round the waist. The bell swings, silent. Get her back to the rope, or give the rope to someone else.

skillChecks.success: If the bell goes on swinging after the twenty-seventh name, and Ardelia says 'One more': you have Zeb's book on the table, and you open it to the flyleaf and run your finger down it against the list, and there it is, the one name that is nowhere else: Asahel Wyman. Ellery Wyman reads it aloud in a cracked voice, and his great-great-uncle, a young man in a fisherman's smock at the edge of the water, looks up. (If the party did not bring Zeb's book or Vining's letter, Thankful Lunt, in her wheelbarrow, remembers: 'There was a Wyman, the first November. Zeb's mother's cousin said. Asa something.' Ellery: 'Asahel. There's a stone.')
skillChecks.failure: The list on the table has twenty-seven names and you read it again and again and they are all there. Ask someone. Ask the old woman in the wheelbarrow. Ask the First Selectman about his family's stones. The tide is turning.

scenes.name: The Last Stroke
scenes.description: When the twenty-eighth name is spoken and rung, the bell swings once more by itself, and stops. And from under the sea, out on the Shelf, where the drowned church still stands empty with its doors open, there comes a single stroke of no bell at all: enormous, soft, felt more than heard, like a great door closing gently a long way off. Then silence. Everyone present drops to 0 Dread. The dead on the slope turn, all together, and walk, not down into the sea but along the shore and up onto the Bar, in a long line among the island's lanterns, past the living, who step aside for them; and as they pass the five lights at the head of the Bar, the lights go out one by one, and the dead are not there. Ardelia Vining is last. She stops by Orpha Sprague, and Orpha, who can hardly stand, says 'I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I should have come,' and Ardelia Vining puts her wet hand for a moment against the old woman's cheek, and goes. Then the epilogue: the island going home along the Bar in the moonlight, nobody speaking; the Store stove at midnight with every chair full and Galen's whisky going round; the first snow on the spruce in the morning; the mail boat on Friday 14 November going out in a light fog, with whoever is leaving at the rail, and behind them the fog bell at the Head, striking every twenty seconds, and no other bell at all.
scenes.readAloud: Asahel Wyman. The bell rings, and swings back, and swings once more by itself, and is still. For a moment nothing happens. Then, from far out under the moonlit water, from the Shelf, from the empty church with its open doors, there comes one stroke of a bell that is not a bell: so deep and so soft that you feel it in your chest more than you hear it, like a door a long way off being closed, very gently, by someone who does not want to wake the house. And then there is no sound at all on Carrow but the sea breathing on the shingle. Down on the slope the dead turn, all of them, together, and begin to walk, not into the water but along the shore and up onto the Bar, a long slow line of them in the moonlight among the lanterns, and the island steps back to let them pass, and nobody is afraid. At the head of the Bar the five small lights are going out, one, and another, and another. The last of the dead is a slight woman in grey, who stops beside an old woman in black silk held up between her great-grandson and a Grindle, and puts out her hand.

skillChecks.success: It is over. You know it the way you know a fever has broken. Everyone around you knows it too: you can see it in their faces, a hundred and forty people letting go of a breath they have been holding for fifty-three years.
skillChecks.failure: You do not trust it yet. You will, in a day or two, when the next big tide comes and goes and nothing rings.

skillChecks.success: Somebody has to start the hymn on the walk back along the Bar, and it is you, and the whole island takes it up. Or Imogen Lisle sings 'The Carrow Bell', all four verses, at the Store stove at midnight, and when she gets to the last, the old people sing it with her, and Thankful Lunt sings the word 'doors'.
skillChecks.failure: Nobody sings. It does not matter. Everyone walks home together.

skillChecks.success: At the Store stove at midnight, Marcellus Tibbetts, Hosea Farr, Galen Coombs and Ellery Wyman, one after another, without anyone asking them, say that their families will give back the Point privilege to the Point families' heirs as Orpha did. Mattie Grindle says she does not know what she will do with it all. Oren Pinkham writes in the log: 'Nov. 13. Full moon. Low water 6.04 p.m. Bell not heard.' And closes it.
skillChecks.failure: The families say nothing about the Point tonight. In the spring, one by one, they will.

encounters: The dead on the slope (all the Drowned of Carrow): they do not attack anyone; they stand, listen and, at the end, go
The call on the ringer and on everyone of the blood in the crowd: Charisma saves and holding, never violence
Ardelia Vining, last: no statistics needed

npcsInvolved.name: Orpha Sprague, 73
npcsInvolved.description: See db-scenario-001. In this scenario she speaks to the island, gives back the Point, and rings for the dead with her own hands, held up by her great-grandson and a Grindle.

npcsInvolved.name: Marcellus Tibbetts, 61
npcsInvolved.description: Lean, grey, deacon's black, owner of the fish weirs on the old Point privilege; Eliphalet Tibbetts's grandson; Clyde's uncle. Decent, proud, frightened for his family's living and his grandfather's name.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Keep the ringing going forever, and the dead decently unnamed. He is not wrong that it would work; he is wrong about the price.

npcsInvolved.name: Lieutenant (j.g.) Harold Scamman, 31
npcsInvolved.description: Tall, tired, courteous, a Bath man in a bridge coat; two years on the rum patrol, two men lost in a fog off Boothbay. Wants to go home with something to write down.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The cable mended, the schooner's master's statement, and a warrant served if he must.

npcsInvolved.name: Myrtle Haskins, 24
npcsInvolved.description: Small, quick, freckled, camel coat, a notebook always open; kind and ambitious in equal parts.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The story of her life, which she will let the island tell her if they tell it well.

npcsInvolved.name: Ellery Wyman, 58
npcsInvolved.description: See db-scenario-001. In this scenario he calls the meeting, owns the Hercules, holds the list to the lantern for Orpha, and reads his own great-great-uncle's name.

npcsInvolved.name: Captain Yves Le Goff, 50
npcsInvolved.role: Master of the wrecked Bonne Chance
npcsInvolved.description: Broad, black-bearded, a Saint-Pierre fisherman turned rum-runner, grateful, courtly and entirely without English; his crew of seven crew the Hercules for nothing.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To get his schooner off the beach, and to repay the island that pulled his men out of the sea.

rewards.money: Merrymeeting Life pays Dr. Thurlow $3,000 on Esther, and Ellery Wyman $1,000 on Jotham, and Len Garrity $200 for Clyde Tibbetts, whatever he wrote. Galen Coombs gives Peg Tolman the Lark's Daughter, his second boat, 'for the bell', and she is worth $1,500. The island gives the party nothing it can put in a wallet, and every one of them, for the rest of their lives, a bed and a supper on Carrow and their name said at the Store stove.
items: The recast Union Church bell, back in its tower, rung by hand on the first Sunday after for a service of thanksgiving and never at the bottom of a tide again
The drowned bell itself, raised, green and black, which the island hangs in a frame on Church Point where it was rung, and never rings
Imogen Lisle's complete recording of 'The Carrow Bell', all four verses, sung by Thankful Lunt
Oren Pinkham's logbook entry, 'Bell not heard', which he shows to anyone who asks
A deed to a share of the Point fishing privilege, for Mattie Grindle
One of the iron spikes from the church doors, for each of the party, which the island asks them to take away

twists: If the doors were buried by Galen's charge on 29 October, the dive in Act 2 must also clear them and draw the spikes under water, over the two spring lows of 11 and 12 November; the dead in the nave press at the cracks as the spikes come out, and the bell calls the diver. It can be done. It should cost a great deal.

Orpha Sprague may die at the end: not killed, but her heart giving out on the frost after the last stroke, peacefully, with Mattie Grindle's hand in hers. The GM should decide only if it fits the table; it is just as good an ending for her to walk home along the Bar on Peleg's arm and live to see the Point families fish the Point again.

If the island would not come (the meeting failed), the rite cannot be done 'before the island', and the bell is not laid; the party can still ring the answer every spring tide, and teach the island to, and leave. That is an honest ending, and the GM should play it as one: the last scene is the next big tide, a young islander climbing the tower with a lantern, and the drowned bell beginning under the sea.

Dr. Thurlow, of the Tibbetts blood, can ring for the Tibbetts names if the reader asks, and should be asked if he has carried his sister out of the church: when he reads 'Esther Thurlow' and pulls, the bell's note is the last thing Esther hears, and she, at the edge of the water, smiles at him.
dmTips: This is the reckoning. The horror is spent; what is left is grief, courage and a decision. Give the town meeting real weight: let Marcellus Tibbetts's reasons be good ones, and let the island choose. A table that has been frightened for three scenarios will be glad to argue.
Read the names aloud at the table, all twenty-eight, one by one. Give each player some to read. It takes four minutes and it is the best four minutes in the campaign.
The Charisma saves on the ringer are not there to make the ending fail; they are there to make the island hold her up. Every failed save is a chance for someone to say 'Orpha' and bring her back.

If the party have the twenty-eighth name, let the bell stop on it and do not mention that it could have gone otherwise. If they do not, Ardelia's 'One more' is the campaign's last clue, and the old woman in the wheelbarrow is there so that they cannot fail it.

Let the epilogue breathe. The Store stove, the hymn, the log, the first snow, the mail boat in the fog. Ask each player what their character does on the last morning on Carrow, and end on the fog bell.
Budget an hour for the week after the storm, an hour and a half for the meeting, the Hercules and the dive, and an hour and a half for the Point, with time for the epilogue.
